analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax deduction corporations get for paying executives over $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 23 House Democrats, has sat in the Ways and Means Committee since May 2025 with no markup and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1993 tax rule caps at $1 million the pay a company can write off as a business expense, but companies dodge it by labeling executives' multimillion-dollar packages as performance-based bonuses. This bill would eliminate that carve-out, apply the $1 million cap to every executive and contractor regardless of job title, cover former top officers, and block companies from dodging it by structuring pay through pass-through entities or by briefly dropping SEC reporting obligations.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who stop footing part of the bill for outsized executive pay. Every dollar of executive compensation above $1 million that a company can no longer deduct increases federal revenue that funds public services or reduces what other taxpayers must cover.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the existing $1 million pay-deduction cap from 'covered employees' to any individual performing services for the company, closing the pass-through and contractor workarounds [S2]
Ends the exclusion that let companies label executive pay as 'performance-based' to deduct unlimited amounts above the cap [S2]
Covers former principal executive and financial officers for years after 2016 and the three other highest-paid officers of those years, so companies cannot restructure to escape the cap [S2]
Blocks avoidance through pass-through entities or by simply ceasing SEC reporting, and applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid executives, who lose the ability to deduct pay above $1 million as a business expense.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public companies and top executives

drawbacks.text: Companies that structure pay as bonuses tied to performance targets would face higher tax bills on compensation above $1 million, raising costs for firms that argue such pay is linked to results [S2]
The look-back rules for former officers and the new regulatory authority add compliance complexity for companies and require Treasury to write detailed rules to prevent workarounds [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill closes a loophole that lets corporations deduct unlimited executive pay above $1 million as an ordinary business expense, shifting that cost to federal taxpayers. The costs fall on large corporations and their highest-paid executives, not on rank-and-file workers or small businesses. The main honest caveat is the compliance complexity of the look-back rules, not who pays: the people currently subsidized are among the highest-compensated individuals in the country.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 1, 2025 by Rep. Lloyd Doggett with 22 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1, S3]
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history shows no further steps, including no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, publicly held corporations and their highest-paid executives continue to deduct pay above $1 million from taxable income, and taxpayers continue to absorb that cost.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations and their highest-paid executives

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand the denial of deductions for excessive employee remuneration [S1, S2]

for.name: 22 House cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Casar, DeLauro, Raskin, Tlaib, and Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction [S3]

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 1, 2025 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill pending in committee [S4]

sides.party_line_note: All 23 backers (the sponsor plus 22 cosponsors) are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; the Ways and Means Committee, which holds the referral, has taken no action.

industries.industry: Publicly held corporations and their most highly compensated executives
industries.note: The bill would strip these companies of tax deductions for executive pay above $1 million, raising their tax bills. Executives' employers currently treat multimillion-dollar pay packages as an ordinary business cost borne partly by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Compensation consulting and executive pay advisory firms
industries.note: These firms design the performance-based pay structures and pass-through arrangements the bill targets; compliance work might grow but the market for structuring deductible excess pay would shrink.

analysis.trajectory: The Ways and Means Committee has not scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill has no Republican cosponsors in a chamber controlled by the majority party's committee leadership. Absent unusual movement or a broad tax package that leadership chooses to include it in, the most likely path is that it sits in committee for the rest of this Congress.
